clue.text: Barrie's address to conspirator?

parts.note: a play by J. M. Barrie whose title is the way one would open a letter to the chief plotter against Julius Caesar

explanation.definitionFit: J. M. Barrie's 1917 play takes its title from Cassius's line in Julius Caesar, a greeting to one of Caesar's assassins.

clue.text: Heard in the night by Brecht

definitions.text: Heard in the night by Brecht

parts.words: Heard in the night by Brecht
parts.note: Brecht's early play is titled '... in the Night', so the thing heard is the percussion instrument of that title

explanation.definitionFit: Brecht's play Trommeln in der Nacht is known in English as Drums in the Night; the singular instrument is what is heard.

clue.text: Whose button came from Darlington?

parts.note: the comic novel and play about a magic button were written by W. A. Darlington, so the owner of that button is the one named in its title

explanation.walkthrough: Darlington looks like the English town, but it is W. A. Darlington, author of the 1919 comic novel Alf's Button.
explanation.definitionFit: In W. A. Darlington's Alf's Button, the soldier Alf owns a button made from Aladdin's lamp, so the possessive names its owner.

clue.text: Entertainment for those with a sweet tooth?

definitions.text: Entertainment for those with a sweet tooth?

parts.words: Entertainment for those with a sweet tooth?
parts.note: a Graham Greene novel shares its title with the stick of seaside candy, so the entertainment is also a sweet

explanation.walkthrough: Greene labelled his lighter books 'entertainments', and this 1938 novel is named after the hard candy sold at the English seaside resort.
explanation.definitionFit: Greene called the novel an entertainment, and the stick of seaside rock it is named after is confectionery.

clue.text: Fate of the Ashes, according to Browne

definitions.text: Fate of the Ashes, according to Browne

parts.words: Fate of the Ashes, according to Browne
parts.note: Sir Thomas Browne's treatise Hydriotaphia, or Urn Burial, concerns cremated remains put into funerary vessels

explanation.walkthrough: The Ashes suggests the cricket trophy, itself kept in a small urn, but Browne is the 17th-century author of Urn Burial.
explanation.definitionFit: Browne's Urn Burial describes cremated remains placed in vessels, the verb used for that being placed in an urn.

clue.text: Boundless as Ballard's instrument of transformation at Shepperton

definitions.text: Ballard's instrument of transformation at Shepperton
definitions.meaning: J. G. Ballard's novel The ... Dream Company transforms the Thames-side suburb of Shepperton

explanation.surface: A description of how far Ballard's imagination remakes his home town.
explanation.definitionFit: Boundless is a plain synonym, and Ballard's The Unlimited Dream Company is the agency that transforms Shepperton in his novel.

clue.text: Could it have preceded Ms Jameson's well-known forename?

definitions.text: Could it have preceded Ms Jameson's well-known forename?

parts.words: Could it have preceded Ms Jameson's well-known forename?
parts.note: the novelist Storm Jameson had a weather first name, and stillness is proverbially what comes before a storm

explanation.definitionFit: The proverb speaks of a lull before the storm, and Storm was Margaret Jameson's pen-forename.

clue.text: Where old Major incited revolution

parts.note: Old Major is the prize boar whose speech starts the uprising in Orwell's fable

explanation.walkthrough: Old Major reads like a retired army officer, but he is the elderly pig in Orwell's novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Orwell's allegory is set on Manor Farm, where the boar Old Major's dream inspires the creatures to rebel.

clue.text: Madrigalist curiously met no opera composer

indicators.note: curiously signals that the letters of met no are arranged in an odd, unexpected order

parts.note: Giuseppe Verdi was the Italian composer of operas such as Aida

explanation.surface: Someone oddly claims they encountered no opera composer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'curiously' turns MET NO into MONTE; then add VERDI.
explanation.definitionFit: Claudio Monteverdi published nine books of madrigals as well as early operas.

clue.text: How Eliot's wise men found the towns

definitions.text: How Eliot's wise men found the towns

parts.words: How Eliot's wise men found the towns
parts.note: in Eliot's poem Journey of the Magi the travellers find 'the cities hostile and the towns' lacking welcome

explanation.definitionFit: Eliot's line pairs hostile cities with towns that were inhospitable, which is how the Magi found them.

clue.text: O'Grady's companionable Scandinavian?

parts.note: Standish O'Grady retold the Irish legends of the hero Fionn and his band of companions, the Fianna; the hero's name also means a native of Finland

explanation.definitionFit: The Irish hero Finn MacCool led a band of companions, and the same name denotes a Nordic-region person from Finland.

clue.text: To Faulkner's mind "the best novel ever written"

definitions.text: To Faulkner's mind "the best novel ever written"

parts.words: To Faulkner's mind "the best novel ever written"
parts.note: Faulkner, asked for the three best novels, named Tolstoy's book about an adulterous wife first

explanation.definitionFit: Faulkner famously called Tolstoy's novel the best ever written.

clue.text: Bragging to make Orlando furious?

parts.note: the boastful Saracen Rodomonte in Ariosto's Orlando Furioso gives English its word for vainglorious talk, and his rivalry enrages the knight

explanation.definitionFit: Boastful talk is named after Rodomonte, the braggart king in Ariosto's epic.

clue.text: Writing equipment said to be at a standstill

indicators.note: said to be shows the word meaning motionless is spoken, giving a word of the same sound

parts.note: something at a standstill is motionless, not moving at all

explanation.surface: A remark that one's pens and paper have stopped working.
explanation.walkthrough: The two spellings sound alike: -ARY means not moving, -ERY means pens, paper and envelopes.
explanation.definitionFit: Paper, envelopes and pens are collectively the materials a writer uses.

clue.text: "And every tree unclothed fast, as nature taught them plain", for example (Surrey)

definitions.text: "And every tree unclothed fast, as nature taught them plain", for example (Surrey)

parts.words: "And every tree unclothed fast, as nature taught them plain", for example (Surrey)
parts.note: the quoted line by the Earl of Surrey has fourteen syllables in seven iambic feet, an example of a metrical form

explanation.definitionFit: A line of seven metrical feet, like Surrey's fourteen-syllable line, is named from the Greek for seven measures.

clue.text: There and back again to win Golden Joystick

definitions.text: There and back again to win Golden Joystick

parts.words: There and back again to win Golden Joystick
parts.note: Tolkien's children's novel is subtitled 'There and Back Again', and its 1982 computer-game version won a Golden Joystick award

explanation.definitionFit: Tolkien's novel carries the subtitle There and Back Again, and the Melbourne House game of it won a Golden Joystick in 1983.

clue.text: "—in beauty " the rolls of black plastic arise (after G. M. Hopkins)

definitions.text: "—in beauty " the rolls of black plastic arise (after G. M. Hopkins)

parts.words: "—in beauty " the rolls of black plastic arise (after G. M. Hopkins)
parts.note: Hopkins's Hurrahing in Harvest says the stooks arise 'in beauty' with a missing adjective; modern wrapped hay bales replace the stooks

explanation.definitionFit: The missing adjective in Hopkins's line means wild and uncivilised, describing the harvest stooks.

clue.text: File a different version of Gilbert production

indicators.note: a different version of a phrase here means its letters reworked into a new order

explanation.surface: An instruction to submit an alternative draft of a stage production.
explanation.walkthrough: Lewis Gilbert directed the 1966 film starring Michael Caine; 'different version of' rearranges FILE A.
explanation.definitionFit: Lewis Gilbert directed the 1966 film about a Cockney womaniser, so it is one of his productions.

clue.text: … and it's goodbye to the right Turkic language

parts.note: ta-ta is an informal British way of saying goodbye

explanation.surface: A trailing farewell to a political party on the right.
explanation.walkthrough: TA-TA is a casual British farewell.
explanation.definitionFit: The language of the Volga people of Tatarstan belongs to the Turkic family.

clue.text: Like members of Conan Doyle league

definitions.text: Like members of Conan Doyle league

parts.words: Like members of Conan Doyle league
parts.note: Sherlock Holmes's story The Red-Headed League concerns a society open only to men with ginger locks

explanation.definitionFit: Conan Doyle's league admitted only men with fiery ginger heads, so its members share that colouring.

clue.text: A best-laid scheme of Steinbeck

parts.note: Burns's poem To a Mouse speaks of the best-laid schemes of small rodents and people, and Steinbeck took his novella title from the line

explanation.definitionFit: Steinbeck's novella title comes from Burns's line about best-laid schemes going wrong.

clue.text: First dramatist, also known as last writer in African capital

indicators.note: First signals taking only the opening letter of the word dramatist
last signals taking only the final letter of the word writer

explanation.surface: Literary gossip about a pioneering playwright who also went by a pen name.
explanation.walkthrough: Take D from 'First dramatist', AKA, and R from 'last writer'; 'in' joins wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The city on the Cap-Vert peninsula is the capital of Senegal.

clue.text: Daughter supporting lyric poem for prophet

indicators.note: in a down clue, supporting means placed beneath, so the daughter comes after the poem

parts.note: an ode is a lyric poem addressing a subject
D is the abbreviation for daughter in genealogies

explanation.surface: A daughter propping up a piece of verse.
explanation.definitionFit: Oded is a Hebrew prophet in 2 Chronicles, father of Azariah.

clue.text: Article about artist (Jack Yeats?) in Synge setting

indicators.note: about here means surrounding, so the article goes round the artist

parts.note: an is the indefinite article
RA, Royal Academician, stands for an artist; Jack B. Yeats illustrated Synge's book on these islands

explanation.surface: An item about the painter Jack Yeats and his work in Synge's island setting.
explanation.walkthrough: The parenthesis is a hint about the artist: Jack B. Yeats illustrated Synge's book The Aran Islands, so the painter belongs in the scene as well as the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Synge's The Aran Islands and his play Riders to the Sea are set on these islands off Galway.

clue.text: Friends of 15's heir in pertinent speech

indicators.note: in shows the letters are found inside the words pertinent speech

explanation.surface: A remark that an heir's friends speak to the point.
explanation.walkthrough: 15 is THE HOBBIT; its heir is Tolkien's sequel, The Lord of the Rings, where the tree-shepherds befriend the hobbits.
explanation.definitionFit: The tree-herds of Tolkien's Fangorn are allies of the hobbits in the sequel to 15.

clue.text: "To treat with a —- to come and gild the backs . . *" (Pepys, Diary, 1666)

definitions.text: "To treat with a —- to come and gild the backs . . *" (Pepys, Diary, 1666)

parts.words: "To treat with a —- to come and gild the backs . . *" (Pepys, Diary, 1666)
parts.note: Pepys records hiring a craftsman to gilt the spines of his volumes; the gap names that tradesman

explanation.definitionFit: The tradesman who sews and covers volumes and gilds their spines fills Pepys's gap.

clue.text: Its sun made glorious summer?

parts.note: Richard III opens with the winter of discontent made glorious summer by this son of a royal house, the sun being a badge of Edward IV

explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's Edward IV is the sun or son of this royal house, punning on his sunburst badge.

clue.text: Tyre change required by him in 677 BC

definitions.text: Tyre change required by him in 677 BC

parts.words: Tyre change required by him in 677 BC
parts.note: an Assyrian king campaigned against the Phoenician city of Tyre and imposed a new treaty on it around that date

explanation.walkthrough: Tyre looks like a car tyre; it is the Phoenician city.
explanation.definitionFit: The Assyrian king who reigned 681-669 BC forced a treaty on Tyre and sacked Sidon in 677 BC.
